title: Tenanted Graceful Yield Policy with KV Temporary Reservation
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Problem: In high-util scenarios our continuous-batching preemptor aggressively evicts tenant KV state and GPU allocations to meet hard SLOs for higher-priority tenants. This causes two problems: (1) cache thrash when the preempted tenant resumes, leading to long tail latency spikes and increased token cost; (2) transient OOMs during preemption handoff because memory accounting is coarse-grained and doesn't distinguish reclaimable KV slabs from pinned model state.

Goal: Implement a tenanted graceful-yield policy that (a) minimizes cache thrashing for preempted tenants by reserving a small temporary KV slab during a configurable grace window, (b) provides short "burst-shield" allowance for tenants to complete in-flight low-latency requests without triggering full preemption, and (c) refines GPU memory accounting to separate soft-evictable KV slabs from hard allocations to avoid unnecessary OOMs. The scheduler should remain SLO-aware (latency percentile and token budget) and be configurable per-customer tier.

Non-goals: This ticket does not change multi-GPU placement or implement cross-node migration. It also does not add new tenant-level billing metrics (follow-up).

Proposed design (high level):
1) KV temporary reservation: when a tenant is selected for preemption, the preemptor marks a small fraction of the tenant's KV cache (configurable, default 8% or 64MB, whichever smaller) as "kv_grace_reserve" and excludes those slabs from immediate eviction for a configurable grace_window (default 3s). The reserved slabs are backed by a soft reference which can be released earlier if overall GPU memory pressure crosses a hard threshold.

2) Burst-shield tokens: each tenant has a burst token bucket (configurable tokens/time). During scheduling, low-latency requests (<= 200ms expected) can consume burst tokens to bypass preemption for short durations. Tokens are replenished on a rate tied to tenant SLA and weight. This prevents expensive preemption for quick interactive flows.

3) Memory accounting refinement: split GPU memory into categories: model_core (pinned), kv_soft (evictable), kv_reserve (temporary reserved slabs), and transient (batch workspace). The preemptor uses kv_soft pressure to make eviction decisions first and only reclaims kv_reserve on hard pressure. We will add per-tenant slab-level reference counts and an approximate LRU aging score to prefer evicting slabs with lowest reuse probability.

4) SLO integration: preemption decisions incorporate a tenant SLO budget vector (p50/p95 latency headroom and token-rate budget). A tenant approaching p95 SLA will be shielded from preemption unless another tenant has higher immediate SLO risk. Policies are weighted by tenant tier (free, standard, enterprise) and a runtime-configurable weight multiplier.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduler honors kv_grace_reserve: reserved slabs are not reclaimed during grace_window under soft pressure.
Burst-shield prevents preemption for sub-200ms interactive requests when tokens available.
No increase in 99th percentile latency for sheltered tenants beyond baseline in our internal perf suite.
Overall memory reclamation still succeeds under worst-case stress (verified by fault-injection tests).
Feature gated behind runtime flag runtime.preemption.grace_reserve and per-tenant config.
E2E integration tests that simulate tenant churn and verify cache hit-rate improvement after preemption-resume cycle (target >= 15% hit-rate delta).
notes: 2026-02-28: Ticket created after postmortem of incident INC-2026-01 where resumed tenants saw sustained latency spikes after preemption.
2026-03-03: Spike experiment on staging shows naive reservation of 128MB reduces resumed-p95 by 28% but increases preemption latency by ~15ms. Need smaller default reserve and soft-reclaim path.
2026-03-05: Design review with runtime team. Agreed to do slab-level reserve, not whole-cache reservation. Action: prototype kv slab tagging and soft-ref counting (ENG-72601).
2026-03-08: UX/PM (Liam) requested per-customer opt-out for burst-shield to avoid fairness exploit by noisy-tenants; decision: allow override in tenant policy with admin flag.

2026-03-10: Initial prototype landed in branch feat/preempt-grace-reserve. Microbenchmarks show ~12% lower token cost after resume in interactive workload. Next: add SLO weight integration and run CI fault-injection tests.
decisions: Use slab-level reservation instead of whole-cache reservation to limit memory overhead.
Default kv_grace_reserve = min(64MB, 8% of tenant_kv) and grace_window = 3s.
Burst-shield tokens apply only to requests tagged as interactive by SDK runtime metadata.
kv_reserve is soft and will be forcibly reclaimed under hard_memory_pressure > 92%.
Expose per-tenant admin override to disable burst-shield and adjust reserve size.
rollout_plan: 1) Canary on 10% of tenants on a single region with synthetic interactive traffic. 2) Monitor resume-p95, cache-hit delta, preemption latency; threshold gates: resume-p95 improvement >=10% and preemption-latency regression <=25ms. 3) Gradual ramp to 50% after 48h, full rollout after 7 days if metrics stable. 4) Provide kill-switch runtime.preemption.grace_reserve.disable=true.
test_plan: Unit tests: slab tagging, soft-ref counting, reserve allocation and early-reclaim path.
Integration: continuous-batcher + preemptor interaction tests that validate reserve semantics under controlled memory pressure.
Fault-injection: simulate OOM path and ensure reserve reclamation prevents node crash.
Load tests: run multi-tenant interactive workload and measure resume-p95 and token cost over 24h.
Chaos: random preemption and tenant churn in staging with observability dashboards.

Run 72h staging ramp with focused interactive traces and collect baseline metrics.
